items.title: 2025-26 Spurs Player Reviews: Harrison Barnes
items.content:
BOSTON, MA - JANUARY 10: Harrison Barnes #40 of the San Antonio Spurs looks on during the game against the Boston Celtics on January 10, 2026 at TD Garden in Boston, Massachusetts. Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2026 NBAE (Photo by David Dow/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images	Welcome to Pounding the Rock’s 2025-26 player reviews! The series will look at the players who finished the season with the San Antonio Spurs on guaranteed contracts and who played consequential minutes and/or a vital role (so no two-way players because we hardly saw them this year, no players who were traded away, and none of the deep bench centers, since they were both irrelevant and are now all gone).

Harrison Barnes2025-26 stats: 77 games, 25.8 MPG, 9.9 points, 2.8 rebounds, 1.9 assists, 38.8 3FG%, 4.6 3PAContract Status: 1 year, $8 million remaining (no options)Age: 34Barnes came into his second season in San Antonio entrenched as a starter and, initially, proved he deserved his spot. He started the season well, posting impressive numbers in October and November for a Spurs team that proved more ready to win than anticipated, even as it battled injuries. Before his inexplicable December-January slump, Barnes was shooting 42 percent from beyond the arc and earning praise on every broadcast because every three-pointer he took looked like it was going in. He was also doing the things expected of him outside his main role as a floor-spacer adequately, but the shooting was his main contribution.

Then December came, and as the days went by, Barnes started to look fallible from outside and not as springy on his drives and on defense. As the new year came in, Barnes was unrecognizable as a shooter, which made the general mediocrity of his other contributions stand out. His subpar rebounding for the position in particular was exposed by Julian Champagnie, who put an emphasis on cleaning the glass and was a more dynamic shooter to boot. Barnes was demoted to the bench, his role declined, and the Spurs might have considered moving on from him, using his expiring contract to get an upgrade at the deadline, if not for the cap constraints adding salary would have represented this summer.  

Eventually, Barnes regained his previous form as a shooter, but by that point things had changed. Champagnie as a starter made it harder for opponents to put a center on Wembanyama, something that happened even when Barnes was hitting shots consistently. Keldon Johnson was slowing down a little but was still on a Sixth Man of the Year run. Carter Bryant was still getting minutes, and by that point starting to actually deserve them. items.title: Nuggets reportedly agree to one-year contract with veteran Lonnie Walker IV
items.content:
Lonnie Walker IV, a seven-year NBA veteran who spent last season with Maccabi Tel Aviv in the EuroLeague, reportedly has agreed to a one-year, $3.3 million minimum contract with the Denver Nuggets to return to the NBA, reports Shams Charania of The Athletic.

Walker is a 6'4" two guard, a position where the Nuggets need depth after losing Tim Hardaway Jr. in free agency (plus Jalen Pickett is not back as well). It's unclear if this contract is fully guaranteed, but it's possible he steps into (or earns the chance in training camp to step into) the role Bruce Brown played with this team.

Walker was a double-digit scorer in four of his seven NBA seasons (four of the last five) and is a career 35.6% shooter from 3-point range. The former No. 18 pick averaged 15.2 points per game in EuroLeague play last season, shooting 35.1% from beyond the arc.

Denver still has a lot of work to do this offseason, most notably either re-signing or finding a sign-and-trade for wing player Peyton Watson. With that comes the fact that the Nuggets are currently already above the second apron of the luxury tax with 12 contracts on their roster — this is a team that needs to shed salary. They have looked for trades for Cameron Johnson or Christian Braun, but would have to add the sweetener of picks to either of them to get another team to take on those contracts at this point in the summer.

Where Walker fits into all that is just another piece of the puzzle.

items.title: Misdemeanor gun charges against James Harden dropped
items.content:
At the request of the Harris County district attorney's office in Houston, a misdemeanor gun charge against Cleveland Cavaliers guard James Harden has been dismissed after he completed an alternative resolution program, reports the Associated Press.

Alternative programs are a fairly common way for people to avoid a criminal record for a minor offense. In this case, Harden likely did some community service in the Houston area, although the agreement did not detail exactly what he did, according to the AP.

Harden, an 11-time All-Star, had been arrested on June 13 for having a gun in the cupholder of his car. He had been driving a car as part of a multi-car group when one of the other drivers was pulled over, according to the Harris County police report. Harden had pulled up behind the police and the other vehicle, and while interacting with the police, one officer noticed Harden had a gun in the cupholder of his car, according to the report. Harden allegedly confirmed the gun was his, which led to his arrest and booking.

Harden played eight seasons — his peak seasons, statistically — in Houston and has close ties to the city. He spends much of his offseason there every year.

Harden, 36, technically still remains a free agent, but is expected to re-sign with the Cavaliers in the coming weeks. He opted out of the $42.3 million he was owed to give the Cavaliers more cap space to chase LeBron James (they struck out there) or make other moves. He is expected to re-sign in Cleveland for around $30 million a season (depending on what other moves the team makes) for multiple years. Harden was traded from the LA Clippers to Cleveland in the middle of this past season, and between the two teams he averaged 23.6 points and 8 assists per game while shooting 37.5% from 3-point range.

items.title: Coroner: Brandon Clarke Died Of Accidental Overdose
items.content:
The Los Angeles County medical examiner’s office announced Friday that Grizzlies forward Brandon Clarke died due to an accidental overdose of heroin and cocaine, writes Melody Gutierrez of The Athletic.

The brief report also cited the “combined effects of multiple prescription medications” as a significant factor in Clarke’s death, Gutierrez adds. Those medications weren’t listed Friday, but will be once the full autopsy report is released in the future, according to the medical examiner.

Clarke spent his entire NBA career in Memphis after being selected with the 21st pick in the 2019 draft. He was 29 years old at the time of his passing on May 11. He was found unresponsive in his bedroom following a 911 call and was pronounced dead by paramedics at 5:15 pm local time, per the examiner’s report. Drug paraphernalia was found at the home and the incident was treated as a possible overdose, which has now been confirmed.

Clarke, who was born in Vancouver, British Columbia, and grew up in Phoenix, was frequently listed as a beloved teammate and was active in the Memphis community. The former San Jose State and Gonzaga standout averaged 10.2 points and 5.5 rebounds while shooting 60.5% from the field in 309 career regular season appearances with the Grizzlies, including 55 starts (20.8 minutes per game).

The Canadian-American was one of the top reserves in the league when healthy, but battled significant injury absences in recent seasons. The 6’8″ power forward missed a little over one calendar year due to a torn Achilles tendon he sustained in March 2023 and was limited to just two games played in 2025/26 due to knee and calf injuries.

Clarke was arrested in Cross County, Arkansas, in April on charges of trafficking a controlled substance, possession of a controlled substance, fleeing in a vehicle exceeding the speed limit, and improper passing. He was released on bond the following day.

Subsequent reporting indicated that over 230 grams of kratom were allegedly found in his possession after he led local deputies on a “miles-long chase” while driving over 100 miles per hour. Kratom, described by the Mayo Clinic as a herbal extract that can act as a stimulant at lower doses and a sedative for pain relief at higher doses, is legal in Tennessee but is considered a Schedule 1 controlled substance in Arkansas.

According to Gutierrez, the coroner’s report didn’t mention whether kratom was present in Clarke’s body at the time of his death.
